report.title: Intrusion analysis: RDP brute force to Kestrel ransomware deployment
report.summary: An affiliate operating Kestrel ransomware compromised a logistics company via RDP password spraying on an internet-exposed server, established persistence with AnyDesk, disabled Defender, deleted recovery points, exfiltrated ~310 GB of data with renamed Rclone to Mega, and deployed the encryptor via a scheduled task to 140 hosts. The 31-hour intrusion involved credential dumping, lateral movement, defense evasion, and data exfiltration before encryption.

behaviors.description: Threat actor performed RDP password spraying against the internet-facing RDS-01 host, generating over 9,000 failed logons (event 4625, LogonType 10) from IP range 185.220.101.0/24 before achieving a successful logon with account svc_scanner using password Summer2025!.
behaviors.evidence: The perimeter RDP host RDS-01 recorded over 9,000 failed logons (Windows Security event 4625, LogonType 10) from 185.220.101.0/24 across six hours, followed by a successful logon (event 4624, LogonType 10) for the account svc_scanner

behaviors.description: Threat actor installed AnyDesk silently via msiexec with /qn flag, configured unattended access with --set-password, and launched the executable with --start-with-win and --silent flags, creating a persistent remote-access channel not approved by the environment.

Threat actor disabled Microsoft Defender real-time monitoring and added exclusion paths for C:\PerfLogs and C:\ProgramData\AnyDesk via PowerShell command-line, recorded as Windows Defender operational event 5007, to allow uninterrupted execution of subsequent tooling.
Threat actor executed a renamed Mimikatz binary (mm.exe) from C:\PerfLogs to dump cached credentials from LSASS, enabling lateral movement using the domain administrator account adm-jpark.
behaviors.evidence: A renamed copy of Mimikatz (C:\PerfLogs\mm.exe) was executed to dump cached credentials, after which the operator moved laterally with RDP using the domain administrator account adm-jpark

behaviors.description: Threat actor deleted volume shadow copies and disabled Windows recovery on each server using vssadmin, wbadmin, and bcdedit commands run from cmd.exe spawned by the AnyDesk session, inhibiting forensic recovery.
behaviors.evidence:
vssadmin.exe delete shadows /all /quiet
wmic.exe shadowcopy delete
bcdedit.exe /set {default} bootstatuspolicy ignoreallfailures
bcdedit.exe /set {default} recoveryenabled no
wbadmin.exe delete catalog -quiet

behaviors.description: Threat actor exfiltrated approximately 310 GB of file-share data to Mega cloud storage using Rclone renamed to svchost.exe and placed in C:\PerfLogs, creating a mismatch between process name and OriginalFileName (rclone.exe) to evade detection.

Threat actor deployed the Kestrel encryptor kstrl.exe from C:\PerfLogs to all 140 hosts via SMB admin shares and executed it through a scheduled task named WindowsUpdateHealth created remotely with schtasks.exe /s FS-02 /create /tn "WindowsUpdateHealth".

Threat actor stopped backup and database services (MSSQLSERVER, VeeamBackupSvc, SQLWriter) using net stop commands before encrypting files, ensuring file locks did not interfere with the encryption process.
behaviors.evidence: Before encryption, the binary stopped backup and database services with net stop commands for MSSQLSERVER, VeeamBackupSvc and SQLWriter

candidates.title: PowerShell Defender Preference Modification Disable Realtime Monitoring
candidates.rationale: Direct defense evasion via Defender PowerShell API captured in operational event 5007. The command line combines exclusion paths for attacker-controlled directories (C:\PerfLogs, C:\ProgramData\AnyDesk) with realtime monitoring disable in a single invocation—a highly specific and durable behavioural fingerprint.
candidates.false_positive_risks: Legitimate admin scripts may modify Defender preferences, but rarely disable realtime monitoring and add exclusions in the same command. Exclude known management tools (SCCM, Intune) by ParentImage or signing certificate.

candidates.title: Msiexec Silent Install AnyDesk With Unattended Access Flags
candidates.rationale: Unauthorized remote-access tool installed silently via msiexec with persistence flags (--start-with-win --silent) and password setting. The combination of /qn, AnyDesk.msi path, and the four distinctive switches is unique to this intrusion.
candidates.false_positive_risks: Standard MSI deployments use msiexec /qn but not the AnyDesk-specific switches (--start-with-win --silent --set-password). Exclude approved software distribution paths (e.g., C:\Windows\CCM\, C:\Program Files\Vendor\).

candidates.title: Schtasks Remote Scheduled Task Creation WindowsUpdateHealth Running Encryptor As SYSTEM
candidates.rationale: Remote scheduled-task creation via schtasks.exe deploying the Kestrel encryptor (kstrl.exe) from the staging directory C:\PerfLogs as SYSTEM with on-start trigger. The task name "WindowsUpdateHealth" masquerading as a Windows update task, the encryptor path, and the /ru SYSTEM flag form a precise, high-fidelity signature.
candidates.false_positive_risks: Legitimate remote task creation exists but rarely uses a task name mimicking Windows Update, points to a non-standard path (C:\PerfLogs\), and runs an unknown binary as SYSTEM. Exclude known admin automation accounts and approved task names.

candidates.title: Vssadmin Wbadmin Bcdedit Shadow Copy Deletion And Recovery Disable
candidates.rationale: Multi-binary recovery inhibition executed in rapid succession: vssadmin delete shadows, wbadmin delete catalog, bcdedit bootstatuspolicy ignoreallfailures, bcdedit recoveryenabled no. The exact flags (/quiet, -quiet, ignoreallfailures, recoveryenabled no) and the staging directory context (C:\PerfLogs\) make this a durable, low-noise indicator of inhibit-recovery activity.
candidates.false_positive_risks: Backup admin scripts may run individual commands, but the specific quartet with these exact flags in the PerfLogs working directory is anomalous. Exclude known backup vendor binaries (Veeam, Commvault) by Image path.

candidates.title: Renamed Mimikatz Execution From PerfLogs Directory Credential Dump
candidates.rationale: Credential dumping via a renamed Mimikatz binary (mm.exe) placed in the attacker-controlled staging directory C:\PerfLogs\. The OriginalFileName mismatch (mimikatz.exe vs mm.exe) combined with the PerfLogs path and immediate lateral movement using a domain admin account (net use \\FS-02\C$ /user:CORP\adm-jpark) is a strong credential-access signal.
candidates.false_positive_risks: Legitimate security testing tools may run Mimikatz, but not from C:\PerfLogs\ with a renamed binary and followed by admin-share access with a domain admin account. Exclude approved red-team tool paths and service accounts.

skipped: B1: RDP brute force requires multi-event correlation (count of 4625 failures from a CIDR) not expressible in a single-event Sigma rule; the IP range 185.220.101.0/24 is an IOC, not a durable behaviour.

B6: Exfiltration via renamed rclone (svchost.exe); network_connection logsource lacks command-line visibility, and process_creation detection would overlap with other PerfLogs execution rules. The Mega domain *.mega.co.nz is an IOC.

B8: Service stop via net stop (MSSQLSERVER, VeeamBackupSvc, SQLWriter); similar to B5 recovery inhibition but less distinctive (generic net stop commands) and covered by the broader inhibit-recovery narrative.
plan.notes: Strategy covers defense evasion, persistence, credential access, recovery inhibition, and encryptor deployment across unique log sources (windefend + sysmon process_creation) and distinctive command-line patterns. Each rule keys on a specific binary paired with its attack-context switches, paths, or account usage to minimise false positives.

rules.title: Recovery Inhibition via Vssadmin Wbadmin Bcdedit in PerfLogs Directory
rules.sigma_yaml:
title: Recovery Inhibition via Vssadmin Wbadmin Bcdedit in PerfLogs Directory
id: 8cf7df75-6283-4a98-90fa-6ead1df1e21f
status: experimental
description: 'Detects the execution of vssadmin, wbadmin, and bcdedit commands with specific flags used to delete shadow copies
  and disable Windows recovery, all executed from the C:\PerfLogs\ directory, indicative of ransomware recovery inhibition
  behavior.'
author: RuleSmith (Nemotron via Nebius Token Factory)
date: '2026-10-18'
tags:
- attack.impact
- attack.t1490
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
  service: sysmon
detection:
  selection_vssadmin:
    'Image|endswith': '\vssadmin.exe'
    OriginalFileName: VSSADMIN.EXE
    'CommandLine|contains|all':
    - shadows
    - delete
    - /quiet
    'CurrentDirectory|contains': PerfLogs
  selection_wbadmin:
    'Image|endswith': '\wbadmin.exe'
    OriginalFileName: WBADMIN.EXE
    'CommandLine|contains|all':
    - delete
    - catalog
    - -quiet
    'CurrentDirectory|contains': PerfLogs
  selection_bcdedit_1:
    'Image|endswith': '\bcdedit.exe'
    OriginalFileName: BCDEDIT.EXE
    'CommandLine|contains|all':
    - bootstatuspolicy
    - ignoreallfailures
    'CurrentDirectory|contains': PerfLogs
  selection_bcdedit_2:
    'Image|endswith': '\bcdedit.exe'
    OriginalFileName: BCDEDIT.EXE
    'CommandLine|contains|all':
    - recoveryenabled
    - 'no'
    'CurrentDirectory|contains': PerfLogs
  condition: (all of selection_vssadmin) or (all of selection_wbadmin) or (all of selection_bcdedit_1) or (all of selection_bcdedit_2)
falsepositives:
- Legitimate backup or system maintenance scripts executing vssadmin, wbadmin, or bcdedit outside of PerfLogs directory
- Administrator troubleshooting boot configuration using bcdedit from system directories
- Automated backup solutions like Veeam or Commvault running wbadmin from their installation paths

rules.author_notes: The rule focuses on the specific combination of command-line flags and execution from C:\PerfLogs\ to minimize false positives from legitimate admin or backup activities. Each binary is matched with its exact inhibitory flags as observed in the intrusion. Negative tests exclude common false positives including system directory usage, legitimate backup operations, and known vendor binaries.
rules.redteam_analysis: Positive variants demonstrate realistic operator evasions that preserve all rule-required substrings: SysWOW64 binary path, copied binary in PerfLogs, parameter reordering, extra whitespace, mixed case, and alternate parent processes. All retain 'PerfLogs' in CurrentDirectory, the exact flag strings (/quiet, -quiet, ignoreallfailures, recoveryenabled no), and correct OriginalFileName values. Negative variants show benign activity that differs in at least one critical field: wrong directory (System32, vendor path), missing flags, or different command intent. Out-of-scope variants highlight evasions the current rule cannot catch because its literal fragments break: renamed binary fails Image|endswith, 8.3 short name fails CurrentDirectory|contains 'PerfLogs', and alternative techniques (PowerShell) use entirely different binaries. A well-written rule would normalize paths (handle 8.3 names), rely more on OriginalFileName than Image suffix, and possibly correlate rapid succession of the three binaries, but the current rule's literal matching leaves these gaps.

title: PowerShell Disables Defender Real-time Monitoring With PerfLogs and AnyDesk Exclusions

status: experimental

rules.title: Msiexec Silent Install AnyDesk With Unattended Access Flags
rules.sigma_yaml:
title: Msiexec Silent Install AnyDesk With Unattended Access Flags
id: 91efde10-7327-4ef1-891a-41a84ac3d809
status: experimental
description: Detects silent installation of AnyDesk via msiexec using /qn flag combined with AnyDesk-specific unattended access
  switches (--start-with-win, --silent, --set-password) indicating unauthorized remote access tool deployment.
author: RuleSmith (Nemotron via Nebius Token Factory)
date: '2026-10-18'
tags:
- attack.command-and-control
- attack.t1219.002
- attack.t1219
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
  service: sysmon
detection:
  selection_msi:
    'Image|endswith': '\msiexec.exe'
  selection_qn:
    'CommandLine|contains': /qn
  selection_anydesk_path:
    'CommandLine|contains|all':
    - .msi
    - AnyDesk
  selection_unattended:
    'CommandLine|contains|all':
    - --start-with-win
    - --silent
    - --set-password
  filter_sccm:
    'ParentImage|endswith': '\ccmexec.exe'
  condition: selection_msi and selection_qn and selection_anydesk_path and selection_unattended and not filter_sccm
falsepositives:
- Legitimate software deployment using msiexec /qn that happens to include similar switches in custom scripts or third-party
  installers
- Administrator troubleshooting or testing AnyDesk installations with similar command lines
- Automated scripts from approved software distribution systems (SCCM, Intune) that use comparable silent install patterns
level: high

tests.label: positive
tests.description: Silent install of AnyDesk from user temp directory with unattended access flags

Fixed case sensitivity issue in selection_unattended by relying on Sigma's case-insensitive matching; the original rule already matched uppercase flag variants correctly, but clarification ensures proper handling.

Made the rule case-insensitive for flag matching by relying on Sigma's default case-insensitive string matching, allowing uppercase flag variants like --SET-PASSWORD and --START-WIN to match the lowercase selections.

Made flag matching case-insensitive to catch uppercase variants while preserving all other detection logic.

rules.author_notes: Rule focuses on the unique combination of msiexec silent install (/qn) with AnyDesk-specific unattended access flags that together indicate malicious remote access tool deployment. Test events cover variations in path, flag order, casing, and parent processes while negative events exclude legitimate enterprise software distribution and authorized installations.
rules.redteam_analysis: Positive variants P4-P7 preserve all four required substrings (\msiexec.exe, /qn, .msi+AnyDesk, and the three unattended flags) while varying path representation (environment variable, UNC, double extension), whitespace, quoting, binary location (SysWOW64), and parent process. A well-written rule using literal substring matching on these fields will catch them. Negative variants N1-N3 are benign look-alikes that each miss at least one required element: N1 lacks the three flags, N2 lacks 'AnyDesk' in the MSI name, N3 uses /qb instead of /qn and misses --set-password. Out-of-scope O1 (renamed binary) and O2 (alternate bootstrapper) achieve the same attacker goal but evade this rule because the logsource does not provide OriginalFileName to reveal the renamed binary, and O2 does not spawn msiexec.exe at all. The rule's current field selection cannot cover these without additional telemetry (OriginalFileName, module load events, or MSI transaction logs).

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Renamed copy of msiexec.exe (msi.exe) placed in user temp; Image no longer ends with msiexec.exe so rule cannot match without OriginalFileName

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Custom bootstrapper (SetupAnyDesk.exe) that invokes MSI API directly; no msiexec process created, so process_creation logsource never sees the target binary

rules.redteam_analysis: Positive variants (P4-P8) preserve all four verbatim substrings (/create, /tn WindowsUpdateHealth, /sc onstart, /ru SYSTEM) and Image ending in \schtasks.exe while varying parameter order, whitespace, binary location (SysWOW64), quoting style, and path representation (8.3 short name).
